title: Common Variant Genotyping: Factor V Leiden, HFE C282Y and Why Not MTHFR
summary: Learn how factor V Leiden causes APC resistance and how it is screened and confirmed, what HFE C282Y homozygosity does and does not mean for hereditary hemochromatosis, and why MTHFR variants are no longer part of thrombophilia testing.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 72 Hits 7 (factor V Leiden) and 9 (hereditary hemochromatosis) and Exam Trap 3 (MTHFR 677C>T is not a standard thrombophilia test). Checked against Nakashima & Rogers 2014, Khan & Dickerman 2006, the BSH 2022 thrombophilia guideline, the ASH 2023 thrombophilia-testing guideline, Deloughery 2022 and the AASLD 2011 hemochromatosis guideline (the ACG 2019 guideline was not read; only a one-page summary is open access). Leiden prevalence and fold-risk figures are taught as ranges because studies differ; the reviewer’s “lifetime penetrance only ~10%” was not found in any source read and is not taught (rv-fvl-ch72-penetrance). The reviewer’s “questionable” MTHFR association is taught as “not associated” per 2022–2023 guidance (rv-mthfr-not-thrombophilia). Not taught: the Number Vault HFE carrier “1 in 8” (AASLD gives about 1 in 10 for C282Y heterozygotes) and the H63D “~20%” carrier figure.

objectives: Explain how factor V Leiden (R506Q) causes activated protein C resistance and state its approximate prevalence and relative thrombosis risks.
Describe the APC-resistance ratio screen, its interferences, and confirmation by DNA genotyping.
Interpret HFE C282Y and H63D genotypes in the context of transferrin saturation and ferritin.
Explain why MTHFR polymorphism testing is excluded from thrombophilia workups.

scenes.title: Three genotype reports
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three genotype reports land on one desk — (1) a 34-year-old with an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis: factor V Leiden (F5 R506Q) heterozygous; (2) the same patient’s panel also lists MTHFR 677C>T homozygous (TT); (3) a 45-year-old man with transferrin saturation 62% and raised ferritin: HFE C282Y/C282Y. Question token: “Which result matters, and how much?”

cues.text: Three genotype reports arrive. A young adult with an unprovoked clot is heterozygous for factor V Leiden.
The same thrombophilia panel also reports a homozygous MTHFR variant.
And a man with high transferrin saturation is homozygous for HFE C282Y. Which result matters, and how much?

props.label: Which result matters, and how much?

scenes.title: Factor V Leiden: a brake APC cannot cut
scenes.altText: Schematic: activated protein C (APC) normally switches off factor Va by cutting it at three arginines (R306, R506, R679). Factor V Leiden (F5 G1691A) swaps arginine 506 for glutamine (R506Q), so factor Va resists APC: activated protein C resistance. Prevalence card: heterozygous in roughly 3–7% of people of European ancestry (figures differ by study), rare in African and South Asian populations. Risk card: venous thrombosis risk about 4–8-fold in heterozygotes (about 5-fold in a 2022 guideline) and about 80-fold in homozygotes; arterial risk unclear.

cues.text: Activated protein C switches off factor five-a by cutting it at three arginine sites. Factor V Leiden changes arginine five-oh-six to glutamine, so that cut fails.
Factor five-a stays active longer. In plasma this shows up as activated protein C resistance.
Factor V Leiden is common in people of European ancestry, roughly three to seven percent are heterozygous, and it is rare in African and South Asian populations.
Venous thrombosis risk rises about four- to eight-fold in heterozygotes and about eighty-fold in homozygotes. Estimates vary by study.

scenes.title: HFE C282Y and the MTHFR exception
scenes.altText: HFE card (AASLD 2011): C282Y (cysteine to tyrosine at 282) homozygotes make up about 80–85% of typical hereditary hemochromatosis; about 1 in 250 white people are C282Y homozygous, but fewer than 10% of them develop severe iron overload with organ damage. C282Y heterozygotes (about 1 in 10) are not at risk of progressive overload; H63D and S65C matter mainly as compound heterozygotes with C282Y. Order: transferrin saturation ≥45% or ferritin above the upper limit → HFE mutation analysis. MTHFR card: 677C>T and 1298A>C are very common (one variant in 60–70% of people); large trials of B-vitamin lowering of homocysteine did not reduce recurrent thrombosis; ACMG, ACOG and BSH advise against MTHFR testing, and the ASH 2023 guideline leaves it out of the thrombophilia panel.

cues.text: Hereditary hemochromatosis is mostly HFE C282Y homozygosity: about eighty to eighty-five percent of typical patients. About one in two hundred fifty white people are homozygous, yet fewer than ten percent develop severe iron overload.

A single C282Y copy, carried by about one in ten, does not cause progressive overload. H63D and S65C matter mainly when paired with C282Y. Testing follows the phenotype: transferrin saturation of forty-five percent or more, or a high ferritin.
MTHFR is the exception. Its common variants are carried by most people, and homocysteine-lowering vitamins did not prevent repeat clots.
Major guidelines now say MTHFR testing should not be part of a thrombophilia workup.

scenes.title: Screen, confirm, interpret
scenes.altText: APC-resistance ratio card: aPTT with added APC divided by aPTT without; about ≥2.0 normal, 1.5–2.0 typical of Leiden heterozygotes, below 1.5 typical of homozygotes — each lab sets its own cutoff. False-low ratios: high factor VIII, low protein S, lupus anticoagulant, heparin, warfarin, direct thrombin inhibitors. Second-generation assay: patient plasma diluted in factor V-deficient plasma, more sensitive and specific. Abnormal screen → DNA genotyping (PCR-RFLP, allele-specific PCR), which detects only the targeted variant. Hook answers: (1) Leiden heterozygote: real, modest risk factor; (2) MTHFR TT: not a thrombophilia, reassure; (3) C282Y/C282Y with high TS and ferritin: consistent with HFE hemochromatosis; ferritin above 1000 µg/L raises concern for cirrhosis.

cues.text: In the lab, a functional screen comes first. The aPTT is run with and without added activated protein C. A ratio near two or above is normal; lower ratios suggest Leiden. Each lab sets its own cutoff.

High factor eight, lupus anticoagulant and anticoagulant drugs can falsely lower the ratio. Diluting patient plasma in factor five-deficient plasma improves the screen. An abnormal screen is confirmed by DNA genotyping, which finds only the variant it targets.
Back to the hook. The Leiden heterozygote has a real but modest risk factor. The MTHFR result is not a thrombophilia, so the patient can be reassured.
And C282Y homozygosity with high saturation and ferritin fits HFE hemochromatosis. A ferritin above one thousand raises concern for cirrhosis.

props.title: Hook answers

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “MTHFR 677C>T is a standard thrombophilia test” (✓ not associated with venous thrombosis; guidelines advise against testing); “A C282Y heterozygote has hemochromatosis” (✓ heterozygotes are not at risk of progressive iron overload); “A high ferritin proves iron overload” (✓ ferritin rises with inflammation and liver disease; pair it with transferrin saturation).

cues.text: Trap one: MTHFR is a standard thrombophilia test. No: its variants are not linked to venous thrombosis, and guidelines advise against testing.
Trap two: one C282Y copy means hemochromatosis. No: heterozygotes are not at risk of progressive iron overload.
Trap three: a high ferritin proves iron overload. No: inflammation and liver disease raise ferritin too, so pair it with transferrin saturation.

props.title: ✗ “MTHFR is a standard thrombophilia test.”
lines: ✓ Not linked to VTE; leave it off

scenes.title: Jammed brake, two keys, a key to nothing
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Factor V Leiden is a JAMMED BRAKE that APC cannot release; HFE hemochromatosis is a vault that needs TWO C282Y KEYS; MTHFR is a key most people carry that opens NO door.” Tokens: jammed brake = Leiden · two keys = C282Y/C282Y · key to nothing = MTHFR. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: factor V Leiden is a jammed brake that activated protein C cannot release. HFE hemochromatosis is a vault that needs two C282Y keys. MTHFR is a key most people carry that opens no door.
Where it breaks: two C282Y keys usually do not open severe disease; a C282Y and H63D pair can open it a little; and a jammed brake raises risk without making a clot certain.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Leiden: APC-resistance screen → genotype · ~4–8× heterozygous, ~80× homozygous”, “HFE: C282Y/C282Y explains most HH, most never severe · MTHFR: leave it off the panel”.

cues.text: Factor V Leiden is a real but modest clotting risk that an APC-resistance screen flags and genotyping confirms, HFE C282Y homozygosity explains most hereditary hemochromatosis but rarely causes severe disease, and MTHFR variants, though very common, are not linked to clots and do not belong on a thrombophilia panel.

HFE: C282Y ×2, mostly not severe · MTHFR: off the panel

explanation.what: Plain language: some gene variants are common in healthy people. Factor V Leiden makes a clotting factor harder to switch off and modestly raises clot risk; two copies of the HFE C282Y variant explain most inherited iron overload, though most people with them never get badly ill; MTHFR variants are very common, are not linked to clots, and testing for them mainly causes worry and confusion. Scientific terms: activated protein C (APC) resistance, F5 G1691A (R506Q), relative risk, APC-resistance ratio, factor V-deficient plasma dilution, PCR-RFLP and allele-specific PCR, HFE C282Y/H63D/S65C, compound heterozygote, transferrin saturation (TS), ferritin, penetrance, MTHFR 677C>T and 1298A>C, homocysteine.
explanation.why: APC normally inactivates factors Va and VIIIa; Leiden factor Va resists cleavage at arginine 506, so thrombin generation is prolonged. HFE C282Y homozygosity predisposes to iron loading, but expression is incomplete and more frequent in men than in women, so genotype and iron phenotype are read together. MTHFR variants raise homocysteine only modestly and mainly in low-folate states, and lowering homocysteine did not change thrombosis outcomes.
explanation.measure: Leiden: functional APC-resistance ratio (aPTT with APC ÷ without; about ≥2.0 normal, 1.5–2.0 typical heterozygote, <1.5 typical homozygote, lab-specific cutoff), false-low with high factor VIII, low protein S, lupus anticoagulant, heparin, warfarin or direct thrombin inhibitors; second-generation assay dilutes plasma in factor V-deficient plasma; abnormal screen confirmed by DNA genotyping. HFE: TS ≥45% or ferritin above the upper limit → HFE mutation analysis; ferritin >1000 µg/L flags cirrhosis risk. MTHFR: not tested in thrombophilia workups.
explanation.differs: Leiden heterozygote (~4–8× venous risk) vs homozygote (~80×); C282Y/C282Y (most HH) vs C282Y/wild type (no progressive overload) vs C282Y/H63D (can be associated with iron loading); a genuine inherited thrombophilia (Leiden, prothrombin 20210A, antithrombin, protein C and S deficiency) vs a common polymorphism without thrombotic association (MTHFR).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the next step after a low APC-resistance ratio, which HFE genotype fits hemochromatosis, why a carrier of one C282Y copy can be reassured, whether a high ferritin alone proves overload, and which thrombophilia test should not be ordered.

questions.stem: A patient’s APC-resistance ratio is 1.7 (laboratory cutoff 2.0). The patient is not on anticoagulants and the lupus anticoagulant screen is negative. What is the best next step?

options.text: Confirm with DNA genotyping for factor V Leiden
options.rationale: Correct. An abnormal functional APC-resistance screen is confirmed by DNA analysis such as PCR-RFLP or allele-specific PCR.

options.text: Report the patient as homozygous for factor V Leiden
options.rationale: Incorrect. A ratio of 1.5–2.0 is typical of heterozygotes, and zygosity is assigned by genotyping, not the ratio alone.

options.text: Add MTHFR 677C>T testing to explain the result
options.rationale: Incorrect. MTHFR variants do not cause APC resistance and should not be part of thrombophilia testing.
Incorrect. A low APC-resistance ratio points to a factor V defect; protein C deficiency is assessed with protein C assays.

questions.stem: A man has transferrin saturation 65% and raised ferritin. Which HFE genotype best explains typical hereditary hemochromatosis?

options.rationale: Correct. C282Y homozygosity accounts for about 80–85% of typical hereditary hemochromatosis.
Incorrect. C282Y heterozygotes are not at risk of progressive or symptomatic iron overload.
Incorrect. H63D heterozygotes are generally not at risk of progressive iron overload.
Incorrect. S65C is generally not iron loading unless paired with C282Y.

questions.stem: After an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis, a patient asks to add MTHFR 677C>T to his thrombophilia panel. What is the best response?

options.text: Explain that MTHFR variants are not associated with venous thrombosis and are not tested in a thrombophilia workup
options.rationale: Correct. ACMG, ACOG and BSH advise against MTHFR testing for thrombosis, and the ASH 2023 guideline describes these variants as not associated with VTE.

options.text: Test, and start folate and B vitamins if he is homozygous
options.rationale: Incorrect. Large randomized trials of homocysteine lowering did not reduce recurrent thrombosis.

options.text: Test, because a homozygous result doubles the anticoagulation duration
options.rationale: Incorrect. MTHFR status is not a thrombophilia and does not guide anticoagulation.

options.text: Order MTHFR instead of factor V Leiden, because it is more common
options.rationale: Incorrect. How common a variant is does not decide the test: MTHFR variants are not associated with venous thrombosis, whereas factor V Leiden is a genuine risk factor.

claims.text: Leiden R506Q resists APC cleavage, causing APC resistance.
Heterozygous in roughly 3–7% of European-ancestry populations; ~4–8× heterozygous and ~80× homozygous venous risk (BSH ~5×).
Reviewer: lifetime penetrance of factor V Leiden only ~10%.
claims.note: Not found in any source read; not taught.

claims.text: APC-resistance ratio cut-offs, interferences, factor V-deficient plasma dilution, confirmation by genotyping.
C282Y homozygotes 80–85% of HH; 1 in 250; < 10% severe; heterozygotes not at risk; H63D/S65C; TS ≥45% or ferritin trigger; ferritin and inflammation; ferritin > 1000.
MTHFR variants very common, not associated with VTE, B-vitamin trials negative, guidelines exclude MTHFR from thrombophilia testing.
“Jammed brake, two keys, a key to nothing.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 72 Hit 7 gives factor V Leiden as 5–7% of whites, ~7× heterozygous risk and “lifetime penetrance only ~10%”. Nakashima & Rogers 2014 give heterozygous prevalence ~3–5% in Caucasians and 4–8× heterozygous risk; Khan & Dickerman 2006 give 3–7% and 7×; the BSH 2022 guideline gives ~5× for a first venous thrombosis. No source read in this session states a ~10% lifetime penetrance; Khan & Dickerman instead cite an estimate that homozygotes can be expected to have at least one venous thromboembolic event in their lifetime, and a family study in which at least 25% of affected carriers had a thrombosis by age 50, so that figure is not taught (register flag rv-fvl-ch72-penetrance).

Ch. 72 Trap 3 calls the MTHFR 677C>T thrombotic association “questionable” and the test “largely dropped”. Deloughery 2022 (with the World Thrombosis Day Steering Committee) states the polymorphisms are not risk factors for venous or arterial thrombosis and should not be in any thrombophilia panel, and the ASH 2023 guideline describes them as shown not to be associated with VTE. The reviewer’s advice is right; the wording understates the evidence (register flag rv-mthfr-not-thrombophilia).
